name: Longest Chain Rule
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Trust the Branch That Worked the Hardest
lesson.summary: The longest chain rule tells every node which competing version of the ledger to treat as canonical: the one representing the greatest total accumulated proof of work, not merely the one with the most blocks.
lesson.body:
Forks happen. Two miners in different parts of the world can find valid blocks within seconds of each other, each unaware of the other's success, and each block gets propagated to different parts of the network first. For a brief window, the network genuinely disagrees about which block comes next. Since a distributed system with no central authority cannot simply have someone declare a winner, it needs a rule that every node can apply independently and still arrive at the same answer. That rule is commonly called the longest chain rule, though the name is a slight oversimplification of what actually happens.

The more precise version, and the one that matters for accuracy, is that nodes follow the chain representing the greatest cumulative proof of work, meaning the sum of the difficulty of every block in that chain, not simply whichever chain happens to contain the most blocks. In practice, because difficulty adjustment keeps block intervals roughly constant, chain length and cumulative work usually track each other closely, which is why the shorthand name stuck. But if difficulty varied meaningfully between competing branches, a shorter chain with harder blocks could in principle outweigh a longer chain of easier ones. Proof of work is the property actually being measured; block count is just a convenient proxy most of the time.

When a node observes a competing branch with more accumulated work than the one it currently considers canonical, it performs what is called a reorganization: it switches to following the heavier branch, and any blocks on the branch it abandons become orphaned. Transactions that were only recorded in those orphaned blocks are not lost forever; they typically return to the pool of pending transactions and can be included in a future block on the now-canonical chain, assuming they remain valid.

A concrete walk-through helps make this tangible. Suppose a miner in one region finds a valid block and a miner elsewhere finds a different valid block just afterward, both extending the same previous block. For a short time, roughly half the network might see one version first and half might see the other, creating a genuine one-block fork. Nothing is resolved by argument or vote. Instead, mining simply continues on both branches until some miner, anywhere in the network, successfully extends one of them with a new block. The moment that happens, one branch has more accumulated proof of work than the other, and every node that was following the now-shorter branch switches over, discarding that branch's single orphaned block.

This rule is what gives proof-of-work blockchains their resistance to rewritten history. An attacker who wanted to replace a block from several confirmations back would need to build an alternative branch from that point forward with more cumulative work than the honest chain has continued to accumulate in the meantime, which generally requires controlling a very large share of total network hashing power. The deeper a block sits beneath the current tip, the more accumulated work stands between it and any rival branch, which is precisely why waiting for additional confirmations after a transaction is considered safer than trusting a single freshly mined block.
